essays.title: A General and His Century
essays.text:
A General and His Century
Douglas MacArthur entered West Point in 1899 and graduated first in his class in 1903. His father, Arthur MacArthur, had received the Medal of Honor for his service in the Civil War. In the First World War he served with the 42nd Division in France and was promoted to brigadier general in 1918. He became Chief of Staff of the United States Army in 1930. During the Second World War he commanded Allied forces in the Southwest Pacific. He accepted the Japanese surrender aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay in September 1945.
In September 1950 he directed the amphibious landing at Inchon, which reversed the opening months of the Korean War. President Truman relieved him of command in April 1951 after a public dispute over how the war should be fought. Days later he addressed a joint session of Congress. One line from that speech is still quoted: “Old soldiers never die; they just fade away.”
He remains the most controversial American commander of the twentieth century. Whatever one thinks of the man, the Inchon landing was a brilliant gamble. He died in 1964.
